fn1.text: Jeddah's water taxi is a live municipal service: inaugurated March 2025 under the city's transport company, connecting the Yacht Club, Historic Jeddah via the port, and Obhur — two air-conditioned vessels, app booking, fares of SAR 25–50 per trip, children five and under free. The Mayoralty has announced an ambition of up to 20 stations.

fn2.text: The Saudi Red Sea Authority is the Kingdom's enabler and regulator of marine and coastal tourism on the Red Sea. Seven regulations published in 2023 cover marinas, marine tourism operators and watercraft classification, and the first tourist-marina operator licenses were issued in 2024 — two of them to Jeddah marinas.

fn3.text: Jeddah Season 2022 drew 6 million visitors in 60 days, including more than a million international guests from 129 countries — official figures.

fn4.text: Route terms in Saudi waters are set with the sailing permit: the Border Guard determines navigational lanes, their speeds and sailing hours, and the Saudi Red Sea Authority identifies routes and navigation maps for marine tourism in coordination with relevant entities. No faster allowance is assumed anywhere on this page.

fn5.text: All map and trip times are planned on a conservative basis: open-coast segments at the vessel's service speed, reduced speed inside Obhur Creek, port waters and every landing approach. Relief appears only as a separately labeled layer.

fn6.text: King Abdulaziz International Airport handled 53.4 million passengers in 2025. Gateway context only: pilgrim flows are inland-bound toward the holy cities and are not counted as water-transit demand anywhere on this page.

fn7.text: Jeddah Central is a published SAR 75 billion, 5.7 million m² central waterfront program with 9.5 km of waterfront including a marina and pier. It renders here as a planned demand trajectory only — nothing on this page relies on its completion, and no completion dates are stated.

fn8.text: Population 3,751,722 in the 2022 Saudi Census — the Kingdom's second-largest city, set along a roughly 30-kilometre coastal waterfront.

fn9.text: Rush-hour congestion costs Jeddah drivers about 43 hours a year, with average city driving speeds near 40 km/h — TomTom Traffic Index, 2025 edition.

copy.headline: Route terms are set with the permit.
copy.framing: Saudi waters run on administrative speed control: the Border Guard sets lanes, speeds and sailing hours in the permit, and the Red Sea regulator maps tourism routes. The purposes are safety, swimmer protection, wake and the reef — outcomes a foiling, electric vessel satisfies inherently.
copy.ask: Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows a rule's purpose is served, set the route's permit terms accordingly — lane by lane, through the process that already exists.

expander.title: What permit terms unlock
body: Saudi speed control separates the number from the purpose: no numeric limit is published for these waters — lanes, speeds and sailing hours are set per route in the sailing permit, and the Red Sea regulator's published mandate is to identify routes and navigation maps for marine tourism. A fast tier is a permit conversation, not a rule change.

Base times on this page assume reduced speed through Obhur Creek, port waters and every landing approach, with foilborne transit only on open coast. Where measurement shows a rule's purposes served, permit terms can shorten creek and near-shore legs — shown here as what terms unlock, never in the base times.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 20 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: Jeddah's water-transport landscape is compact and clearly mandated. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: The city's transport arm — owns and operates the live water taxi connecting the Yacht Club, Historic Jeddah and Obhur, with an announced ambition of up to 20 stations.
Develops and controls the corniche and waterfront — recreational zones, waterfront stages and new public water-access points run through the Municipality.
The Kingdom's enabler and regulator of marine and coastal tourism on the Red Sea — licenses marinas, operators and watercraft, and identifies routes and navigation maps for marine tourism.
The national regulator of passenger transport, including maritime — licenses scheduled marine passenger service and the vessels that run it.
Issues sailing permits and sets navigational lanes, speeds and sailing hours for small craft — route terms are agreed here, permit by permit.

Port landlord at the southern end of the network and a Red Sea cruise homeport. Port waters run under harbourmaster coordination, with the fairway crossed at designated points — the city's water taxi already operates through them today.
Steward of the published SAR 75B central waterfront program, including a marina and pier — a natural mid-corridor landing partner as the program opens.
Promotes Jeddah's leisure waterfront — Obhur marinas, resort-day trips north and corniche experiences — the demand side of these corridors.
